title: Kenyan Cassava Fries
community: Popular on the coast and increasingly nationwide
author: Chef Amina Hassan
desc: Kenyan Cassava Fries — boiled cassava cut into sticks and deep-fried until golden and crispy, then seasoned with salt, chilli, and lemon. A coastal favourite that is crunchier on the outside and softer and creamier inside than potato fries — uniquely satisfying.
longDesc: Cassava fries have a character that potato fries cannot match — the exterior gets crunchier and crispier, while the interior becomes almost creamy and slightly sticky. Seasoned with salt, chilli powder, and a squeeze of lemon after frying, they are deeply addictive and a beloved coastal street snack. Increasingly popular in urban markets across Kenya as an alternative to potato chips.
ingredients: 600g fresh cassava — peeled and cut into thick sticks
steps: Peel cassava and cut into thick sticks — about finger-sized. Remove the woody central fibre.
Boil in salted water for 15—20 minutes until just tender but still holding shape. Do not overboil.
Drain thoroughly and allow to cool and dry completely — at least 20 minutes. The drier the cassava, the crispier the fries.
Fry cassava sticks in batches for 4—5 minutes until deep golden and crispy.
Season immediately with salt, chilli powder, and curry powder. Squeeze lemon juice over.
Scatter coriander if using. Serve immediately.
chefTips: Boiling before frying is essential — raw cassava will not cook through in the frying time.
Allow the boiled cassava to dry completely — surface moisture prevents crispiness.
For extra crispiness, fry twice: once at 160°C for 3 minutes, rest, then again at 190°C for 2 minutes.
commonMistakes: Not boiling first — remains raw inside.
Wet cassava — steams in the oil instead of crisping.
Overcooking during boiling — falls apart in the fryer.

faqs.a: Yes — cassava is naturally gluten-free, making cassava fries an excellent option for those avoiding gluten.

cookingScience: Pre-boiling gelatinises the cassava starch, creating a soft, slightly sticky interior. The subsequent frying dehydrates the exterior surface and causes Maillard browning — the contrast between the crispy exterior and creamy interior is what makes cassava fries distinctive.
sustainabilityTips: Cassava is one of the most drought-resistant crops in Africa.
Using cassava instead of potato diversifies crop demand and supports cassava farmers.
culturalNote: Cassava fries are a coastal street food classic — sold at Mombasa beachside stalls and increasingly popular in Nairobi markets. Their unique texture — crunchier outside, creamier inside than potato — has earned them a dedicated following.
regionalVariations: Classic cassava fries with salt and lemon.
Sweet cassava fries with cinnamon sugar.
